subtopics.title: Absorption, spontaneous and stimulated emission
subtopics.theory_md:
Between levels $E_1<E_2$ with $h\nu=E_2-E_1$ there are three processes.
- **Stimulated absorption**: a photon lifts an atom from $E_1$ to $E_2$.
- **Spontaneous emission**: an excited atom falls to $E_1$ by itself, in a random direction and phase, so the light is **incoherent**.
- **Stimulated emission**: an incident photon of energy $h\nu$ makes the excited atom emit a second photon with the **same frequency, phase, direction and polarisation**. This is the source of laser light.

LASER = Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Laser light is monochromatic, coherent, highly directional and intense.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of a crowd of people shouting at random (spontaneous) against a choir that sings together because one singer cues the next (stimulated).
key_points: Stimulated emission: incident photon produces an identical photon (same frequency, phase, direction)
Spontaneous emission is random, so incoherent
Laser light: monochromatic, coherent, directional, intense

questions.q: Which process gives rise to coherent light in a laser?
questions.why: The stimulated photon copies the phase, frequency and direction of the stimulating photon.

questions.q: Distinguish between spontaneous and stimulated emission. State four properties of laser light.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Spontaneous emission:** the excited atom drops to a lower level without any external agency; photons go in random directions with random phase (incoherent); the rate is $A_{21}N_2$.

**Stimulated emission:** an incident photon of energy $h\nu=E_2-E_1$ induces the atom to emit a photon identical in frequency, phase, direction and polarisation (coherent); the rate is $B_{21}N_2u(\nu)$.

**Laser properties:** (1) monochromatic, (2) coherent, (3) highly directional (very small divergence), (4) very intense.
points: Spontaneous: no external agency, random direction and phase, incoherent
Stimulated: induced by a photon of $h\nu$, identical photon, coherent
Any four laser properties: monochromatic, coherent, directional, intense

subtopics.title: Population inversion and pumping
subtopics.theory_md:
At thermal equilibrium the lower level is more populated (Boltzmann, $N_2/N_1=e^{-h\nu/kT}<1$), so absorption beats stimulated emission and light is attenuated.

**Population inversion** is the non-equilibrium state with $N_2>N_1$. Only then does stimulated emission dominate and the medium amplify light.

It is achieved by **pumping** (optical, electrical discharge, collisions) into a **metastable state**, an excited level with a long lifetime (about $10^{-3}$ s against $10^{-8}$ s for ordinary levels), so atoms pile up there. A three-level system needs strong pumping (over half the atoms lifted); a four-level system inverts easily because the lower laser level empties quickly.
subtopics.basics_md: Water flows downhill by itself. To have more water upstairs than downstairs you must keep pumping it up and give it a tank that holds it. The pump is pumping, the tank is the metastable state.
key_points: Needed for net stimulated emission, i.e. amplification
Achieved by pumping through a metastable state (lifetime about $10^{-3}$ s)
Four-level scheme is easier than three-level

points: $N_2>N_1$: more atoms in the higher level than the lower
Needed for amplification by stimulated emission; achieved by pumping via a metastable state

options: has a long lifetime, so atoms accumulate in it
questions.why: Lifetime of about $10^{-3}$ s lets the population build up.

questions.why: Boltzmann: $N_2/N_1=e^{-h\nu/kT}<1$.

questions.q: Why is population inversion necessary for laser action, and why can it not be reached by thermal means? What is the role of a metastable state?
questions.model_answer_md:
1. At equilibrium $N_1>N_2$, so absorption exceeds stimulated emission and the beam is attenuated.
2. Net amplification needs $N_2>N_1$ (population inversion).
3. Heating only moves the ratio $N_2/N_1=e^{-h\nu/kT}$ towards 1, never above it, so inversion needs **pumping**.
4. A **metastable state** has a long lifetime ($\sim10^{-3}$ s), so pumped atoms stay there instead of decaying at once, allowing $N_2>N_1$.
points: Thermal means cannot invert; pumping is needed
Metastable state has long lifetime so atoms accumulate

subtopics.title: Einstein coefficients and their relation
subtopics.theory_md:
For levels 1 and 2 ($N_1,N_2$ atoms) in radiation of energy density $u(\nu)$:
- Absorption rate $=B_{12}N_1u$
- Spontaneous emission rate $=A_{21}N_2$
- Stimulated emission rate $=B_{21}N_2u$

$A_{21}$, $B_{12}$, $B_{21}$ are the **Einstein coefficients**.

At equilibrium absorption = emission: $B_{12}N_1u=A_{21}N_2+B_{21}N_2u$. With $N_1/N_2=e^{h\nu/kT}$ this gives $u=\dfrac{A_{21}}{B_{12}e^{h\nu/kT}-B_{21}}$. Matching Planck's law $u=\dfrac{8\pi h\nu^3}{c^3}\dfrac{1}{e^{h\nu/kT}-1}$:
$$B_{12}=B_{21},\qquad \frac{A_{21}}{B_{21}}=\frac{8\pi h\nu^3}{c^3}$$
Spontaneous emission wins as $\nu^3$ grows, so high-frequency lasers are hard to build.
subtopics.basics_md: A is the chance an excited atom emits on its own per second. B is the chance per second per unit of radiation density, for absorbing or being stimulated.

topics.topic: Ruby and He-Ne lasers and applications

subtopics.title: Ruby laser
subtopics.theory_md:
**Construction:** a rod of $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ doped with about 0.05% $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$, ends flat, parallel and silvered (one fully, one partly); a helical **xenon flash lamp** around it for optical pumping.

**Working (three-level):** flash lifts $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ from $E_1$ to the broad band $E_3$; fast non-radiative decay to the metastable $E_2$ (lifetime $\sim10^{-3}$ s); inversion between $E_2$ and $E_1$; stimulated emission at **6943 Å** (red), a pulse leaves via the partial mirror.

**Disadvantages:** high pump power (three-level), efficiency under 1%, pulsed output, heating.
**Uses:** holography, ranging, eye surgery, drilling and welding.
subtopics.basics_md: Chromium ions in the ruby crystal are the active atoms. The lamp lights them up, they park in a long-lived level, and then fire together.
key_points: Ruby rod $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ with 0.05% $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$, xenon flash lamp pump
Three-level scheme: $E_1\to E_3\to E_2$ (metastable), lasing $E_2\to E_1$
Disadvantages: high pump power, low efficiency, pulsed

points: Construction: ruby rod ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ + 0.05% $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$), polished silvered ends (one partial), xenon flash lamp
Working: pumping $E_1\to E_3$, non-radiative decay to metastable $E_2$, inversion, stimulated emission at 6943 Å
Disadvantages: three-level so high pumping, under 1% efficiency, pulsed, heating

subtopics.title: He-Ne laser
subtopics.theory_md:
**Construction:** a glass tube (about 30 cm) with He:Ne at about 10:1 and about 1 mm Hg; DC discharge of a few kV between electrodes; two mirrors form the cavity (one fully, one about 99% reflecting) or Brewster windows.

**Working (four-level):** electrons excite He to metastable $2^3S_1$ (19.8 eV) and $2^1S_0$ (20.6 eV). These match Ne $4s$ and $5s$, so resonant collisions pump Ne: **inversion** against $3p$ and $4p$. Lasing $5s\to3p$ gives **632.8 nm** red (also 3.39 $\mu$m, 1.15 $\mu$m). Ne decays $3p\to3s$, then to ground by wall collisions, keeping the lower levels empty.

CW output, 1 to 50 mW, efficiency about 0.1%.
subtopics.basics_md: Helium is the pump and neon is the lasing atom. Helium collects energy from the electric current and hands it over to neon by collision.
key_points: He:Ne about 10:1 at about 1 mm Hg, electrical discharge
He metastable levels $2^3S$, $2^1S$ pass energy to Ne $5s$, $4s$ by resonant collision
Lower levels cleared by $3p\to3s$ decay and wall collisions

points: Labelled diagram: discharge tube with He and Ne (10:1), electrodes with HV supply, full and partial mirrors

Lasing $5s\to3p$ at 632.8 nm; output through partial mirror
Energy level diagram: He $2^3S$, $2^1S$; Ne $5s$, $4s$, $4p$, $3p$, $3s$, ground
Pumping by electron impact then He-Ne collision
Principle: inversion + stimulated emission + mirror cavity

subtopics.title: Principle, recording and reconstruction
subtopics.theory_md:
**Holography** records both **amplitude and phase** of light from an object, giving a 3-D image. Photography records only intensity.

**Recording:** a laser beam is split. The **object beam** is scattered by the object onto a photographic plate; the **reference beam** (from a mirror) falls directly on the plate. Their **interference** pattern, a fringe pattern, is recorded: the hologram. Coherent light is essential (He-Ne is common).

**Reconstruction:** the developed hologram is illuminated by the reference beam alone. It diffracts the light and reproduces the original object wave, giving a **virtual 3-D image** (and a real image).

Holography was proposed by Gabor (1948).
subtopics.basics_md: A hologram is a frozen interference pattern. Shine the reference wave on it again and the pattern re-creates the object wave, so you see the object as if it were there.
key_points: Records amplitude and phase by interference of object and reference beams
Beam splitter, mirror, photographic plate; coherent laser needed
Reconstruction by the reference beam alone
Gives 3-D virtual image; Gabor invented it

questions.q: A hologram stores information about the object's
questions.why: Interference with the reference beam encodes the phase too.

questions.q: A hologram is reconstructed by illuminating it with
options: white light of any kind with no coherence
questions.why: The reference beam is diffracted by the fringes to give the object wave.

questions.q: Explain the recording and reconstruction of a hologram with a diagram.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Recording (diagram described):** a laser beam falls on a beam splitter. One part (object beam) illuminates the object, which scatters it onto the photographic plate. The other part (reference beam) is reflected by a mirror and falls directly on the plate. The two coherent beams interfere and the fringe pattern, containing amplitude and phase, is recorded.

**Reconstruction (diagram described):** the developed plate is illuminated with the reference beam only. The fringes diffract it, reproducing the original object wave. An observer behind the plate sees a virtual, 3-D image at the object's position (a real image is also formed).
points: Beam splitter gives object and reference beams

subtopics.title: Holography versus photography, applications
subtopics.theory_md:

**Applications:** holographic interferometry (stress and vibration analysis), non-destructive testing, data storage, security holograms on notes and cards, art and 3-D displays, pattern recognition.

subtopics.title: Structure and propagation by total internal reflection
subtopics.theory_md:
An **optical fibre** is a thin glass or plastic strand with a **core** (index $n_1$), a **cladding** (index $n_2<n_1$) and a protective buffer or jacket.

Light is guided by **total internal reflection (TIR)** at the core-cladding boundary. TIR needs light to go from denser to rarer medium with angle of incidence greater than the **critical angle**
$$\theta_c=\sin^{-1}\frac{n_2}{n_1}$$
The ray zig-zags down the core with very little loss. Rays entering outside the acceptance cone hit the boundary below $\theta_c$ and leak into the cladding.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of a corridor of mirrors: a ray that hits the wall at a shallow angle bounces forever; a ray hitting steeply escapes.
key_points: Rays outside the acceptance cone are lost

questions.q: For guidance in a fibre the cladding index must be
questions.why: TIR needs light going from higher to lower index.

questions.q: The critical angle at the core-cladding boundary is
questions.why: $\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1<1$.

questions.q: Explain with a diagram how light travels through an optical fibre and state the conditions for TIR.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Diagram (described):** a long cylindrical core of index $n_1$ inside a cladding of index $n_2<n_1$; a ray enters the end face, refracts, and zig-zags by repeated TIR at the core-cladding interface.

**Conditions:** (1) $n_1>n_2$; (2) angle of incidence at the core-cladding boundary $\phi>\theta_c=\sin^{-1}(n_2/n_1)$, which is satisfied only for rays entering within the acceptance angle.

subtopics.title: Acceptance angle and numerical aperture
subtopics.theory_md:
A ray enters the end face from air ($n_0=1$) at angle $\theta_0$, refracts to $\theta_r$ in the core and meets the boundary at $\phi=90^\circ-\theta_r$. The limit is $\phi=\theta_c$, $\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1$.

Snell: $n_0\sin\theta_0=n_1\sin\theta_r=n_1\cos\theta_c=\sqrt{n_1^2-n_2^2}$.

- **Acceptance angle** $\theta_0=\sin^{-1}\!\big(\sqrt{n_1^2-n_2^2}/n_0\big)$: the maximum entry angle for guided rays.
- **Numerical aperture** $NA=n_0\sin\theta_0=\sqrt{n_1^2-n_2^2}=n_1\sqrt{2\Delta}$, with $\Delta=(n_1-n_2)/n_1$.

NA measures light-gathering power. Always: $\theta_c$ first, then NA, then $\theta_0$.
subtopics.basics_md: The acceptance angle is the half-angle of a cone: light shone into the fibre inside this cone is trapped, outside it is lost.
key_points: Acceptance angle: max entry angle for TIR
Derive from Snell at entry and $\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1$

points: TIR zig-zag propagation of rays inside core
Derivation of $NA=\sqrt{n_1^2-n_2^2}$ with critical angle condition
NA defined as $\sin$ of acceptance angle (light-gathering ability); expression $\sqrt{n_1^2-n_2^2}$

subtopics.title: Fibre types, V-number and modes
subtopics.theory_md:
**By index profile:** *step-index* (constant core index, abrupt drop at cladding) and *graded-index* (core index falls smoothly from axis to cladding, rays follow curves, less modal dispersion).
**By modes:** *single-mode* (core about 8 to 10 $\mu$m, one path, no modal dispersion, long-haul, laser source) and *multimode* (core 50 to 62.5 $\mu$m, many paths, LED source, short distances).

**V-number:** $V=\dfrac{\pi d}{\lambda}NA=\dfrac{2\pi a}{\lambda}NA$. Modes: $N\approx V^2/2$ (step-index), $V^2/4$ (graded). Single-mode only if $V<2.405$.
subtopics.basics_md: The V-number says how many 'lanes' light can use. Small V (thin core, small NA, long wavelength) gives one lane.
key_points: Number of modes $N\approx V^2/2$ step-index, $V^2/4$ graded

questions.why: The cutoff of the second mode is $V=2.405$.

subtopics.title: Attenuation and the dB/km numerical
subtopics.theory_md:
**Attenuation** is the loss of optical power along the fibre.
$$\alpha=\frac{10}{L}\log_{10}\frac{P_{in}}{P_{out}}\ \text{dB/km}$$
with $L$ in km. Total loss in dB $=\alpha L$; $P_{out}=P_{in}\times10^{-\alpha L/10}$. Typical silica fibre: about 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm, 0.35 dB/km at 1310 nm; the minimum-loss window is 1550 nm. 3 dB means half the power.
subtopics.basics_md: A decibel is a ratio on a log scale: every 10 dB is a factor of 10 in power, 3 dB is a factor of 2.

questions.q: Attenuation in an optical fibre is usually expressed in
questions.why: Power loss per unit length on a log scale.

questions.q: A 3 dB loss means the output power is about
Light of 2 mW enters a 10 km fibre and 0.5 mW emerges. Find the attenuation coefficient. What power emerges from a 50 km link of 0.4 dB/km fibre fed with 1 mW?
questions.model_answer_md:
$\alpha=\dfrac{10}{10}\log_{10}\dfrac{2}{0.5}=\log_{10}4=0.602$ dB/km.

Link: loss $=0.4\times50=20$ dB, so $P_{out}=1\ \text{mW}\times10^{-2}=0.01$ mW $=10\ \mu$W.

subtopics.title: Causes of fibre loss
subtopics.theory_md:
- **Absorption:** intrinsic (silica UV and IR tails) and extrinsic (impurities such as $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ ions, water peaks).
- **Scattering:** **Rayleigh scattering** from density and composition fluctuations, loss $\propto1/\lambda^4$, the main loss below 1.6 $\mu$m.
- **Bending losses:** *macrobending* (large bends, angle falls below $\theta_c$) and *microbending* (tiny axial kinks from pressure or cabling).
- **Dispersion** (modal, material, waveguide) does not lose power but broadens pulses and limits bit rate.
- Coupling and splice losses.
subtopics.basics_md: Light is lost by being swallowed (absorption), thrown sideways (scattering) or leaking out at bends.
key_points: Absorption: intrinsic and impurity ions ($\mathrm{OH^-}$, metals)

questions.q: Rayleigh scattering loss varies with wavelength as
questions.why: Shorter wavelengths scatter far more.

questions.q: Which causes loss by the ray striking the boundary below the critical angle?
questions.why: At a sharp bend the incidence angle falls below $\theta_c$.

questions.q: List the types of loss in optical fibres and explain any two. By what factor is Rayleigh loss at 0.85 $\mu$m larger than at 1.55 $\mu$m?
questions.model_answer_md:
Losses: absorption, scattering, bending, dispersion, coupling.

**Absorption:** impurity ions ($\mathrm{OH^-}$, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$) and the intrinsic silica tails absorb light and turn it to heat.
**Rayleigh scattering:** density fluctuations frozen in the glass scatter light, $\propto\lambda^{-4}$.

Ratio: $(1.55/0.85)^4=11.1$ times larger.

subtopics.title: Block diagram of an optical communication link
subtopics.theory_md:
**Transmitter:** an electrical signal modulates a light source, a **laser diode** (single-mode, long distance) or **LED** (multimode, short distance), at 850, 1310 or 1550 nm.
**Channel:** the optical fibre, with **repeaters/amplifiers** (EDFA) along long links to restore the signal.
**Receiver:** a **photodiode** (PIN or avalanche) converts light back to current, then amplifier and decoder give the output.

Block diagram: Input signal $\to$ encoder $\to$ modulator + source $\to$ fibre (with repeaters) $\to$ detector $\to$ amplifier/decoder $\to$ output.
subtopics.basics_md: It is the same chain as a telephone line, only the wire is glass and the carrier is light.
key_points: Fibre channel with repeaters or amplifiers

questions.q: Draw and explain the block diagram of an optical fibre communication system.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Block diagram (described):** Information $\to$ encoder/modulator $\to$ optical source (laser diode or LED) $\to$ optical fibre with repeaters $\to$ photodetector (PIN or APD) $\to$ amplifier and decoder $\to$ output.

- **Transmitter:** converts the signal to digital pulses and drives the source, which emits the modulated light.
- **Fibre:** guides the light by TIR; repeaters regenerate the attenuated and dispersed signal.
- **Receiver:** the photodiode converts light to current; the amplifier and decoder recover the original information.

subtopics.title: Advantages and applications
subtopics.theory_md:
**Advantages over copper:**
- Enormous bandwidth, so very high data rate.
- Very low loss (about 0.2 dB/km), so fewer repeaters.
- Immune to electromagnetic interference and no cross-talk.
- Small, light and cheap raw material (silica).
- Secure: hard to tap; no spark hazard.

**Limits:** splicing and connectors are costly and need skill; fibre is brittle.

**Applications:** telephony and internet backbone, cable TV, LAN, medical endoscopy, sensors, military links. Several wavelengths can share one fibre (WDM).
subtopics.basics_md: Light has a far higher frequency than electric signals in wire, so a fibre can carry many more signals at once and with less loss.
key_points: Immune to EMI and cross-talk, secure

questions.q: A major advantage of optical fibre over copper cable is
questions.why: Light signals are not affected by electromagnetic fields.

questions.q: WDM stands for
questions.why: Many wavelengths carried on one fibre.

questions.q: State four advantages of optical fibre communication and two applications.
questions.model_answer_md:
